accuracy.evidence: Asch figures checked against Asch (1956) Psychological Monographs 70(9): about 37% conformity on critical trials, about 75% of participants conforming at least once, and errors falling to about 5.5% with one truthful partner; the lab and text say 'about a third', 'about 3 in 4' and 'about 1 in 20'. The overestimation of peer risk behaviour is from Perkins and Berkowitz (1986) social norms work. Strategies (clear no, humour with a new plan, walking away, telling a trusted adult) match PSHE Association KS2 guidance and the topic's own evidence list. The 'Trust your eyes' rounds are labelled as a re-creation, with the crowd's wrong answer always visibly wrong.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented beliefs: all peer pressure is bad (step 1 prediction, challenge 'helpful', m8), resisting needs a fight or insult (step 4 prediction and the 'attack' option every round, challenge 'attack'), 'just once' does not count (step 2, challenge 'once', p3), 'everyone does it' is true and a reason (step 2, challenge 'norm', m2), staying quiet when a friend is pushed (step 3 ally round, challenge 'quiet', m3), and keeping a secret when someone is hurt (step 5 card, challenge 'secret', m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpeer is built on the mechanism of pressure itself: naming the four pressure tricks in chat messages, a re-creation of Asch's line judgement where five classmates' answers appear one by one and an ally appears in round 3, a pressure bar that rises across three escalating pushes, and a harmless-versus-harmful copying sort. flagcues reads body-language cues and builds assertive replies; flagbully covers bullying roles. The distinct gate passed under 30% similarity to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner experiences the pull before being told: in rounds 1 and 2 every classmate says the wrong line, and picking their answer is refused with 'You went with the crowd. Look at the lines, not the people'; round 3 adds one ally and the success line names the ally effect, with the Asch results shown after. In Hold your line, giving in or insulting is refused with the specific cost, and only calm, humorous or walk-away replies move the push forward.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each carry a tempting wrong answer that the lab disproves: 'peer pressure is always bad' (step 1, disproved by three helpful pushes in the sort), 'almost nobody goes along with a clearly wrong group' (step 3, disproved by the crowd rounds and the 3 in 4 result), and 'insult them back so they stop' (step 4, disproved when the insult reply is refused because it makes the group push harder).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Each wrong challenge answer maps to its own message: 'alone' and 'adult' (what counts as a peer), 'norm' and 'friend' (everyone or a friend saying it is not a reason), 'once' (one time still counts), 'helpful' (mislabelling a harmful push), 'quiet' and 'attack' (what helps against a group), 'secret' and 'spread' (what to do when someone is hurt). Six questions rotate on retry.

readability.evidence: Kid text is FK grade 2.4 against the learner target of 6.5, with each trick named in its own short sentence. Adult text was rewritten from FK 12.4 to 5.3 (target 9.5) by splitting long sentences while keeping the Asch and social norms figures. Lab cards are under 12 words and quote the actual words a child might hear.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph does one job: define peer pressure, separate helpful from harmful, name the four tricks, then the ally finding and three ways to say no. No banned phrases and explanation overlap with every other lesson is under 12%. Each lab feedback line says why that specific reply or card fails, for example 'One time still counts.'

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light for all six steps: push and choice cards wrap to two lines inside an 88% width card, the two sort boxes are half-width each, the four trick tiles sit in a 2 by 2 grid of 56 px targets, the three replies are full-width 54 px rows, and the line test fits the reference line plus A, B and C with letters below and a 'Match me' label added after review. The crowd dots fit five across at 390 px.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme. Every canvas action has a button (Helpful push, Line A, each reply spoken as 'Say: …'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result so screen reader users hear what the crowd said and why a reply failed.

Perkins, H. W. and Berkowitz, A. D. (1986). Perceiving the community norms of alcohol use among students (social norms approach)
